chapter.name: Health: The Ultimate Treasure
chapter.blurb: Defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being, covers healthy lifestyle and environment habits, explains the causes and spread of communicable and non-communicable diseases, and introduces prevention through immunity and vaccines and treatment through antibiotics, including antibiotic resistance.

concepts.name: Health: more than not falling sick
concepts.description: The WHO definition of health as physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease, and why a person needs all three to be truly healthy.
concepts.idea: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease.
concepts.rule: As per the World Health Organization (WHO), health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease. A healthy person can generally perform various tasks more efficiently, cope well in different and difficult situations, and adjust well with peer groups and other members of society. Health also includes feeling good physically, staying positive, and having strong relationships. Being happy helps us stay active and healthy, and good health also improves our mood, so health and happiness are closely related. A person who has no disease but feels lonely, stressed or cannot get along with others is not completely healthy, because mental and social well-being matter just as much as physical well-being.
concepts.example: A student who eats well and has no illness but feels very lonely after moving to a new school is not completely healthy, because his mental and social well-being are affected.

concepts.name: Staying healthy: lifestyle, environment and symptoms versus signs
concepts.description: Habits and surroundings that keep the body and mind healthy, including diet, exercise, sleep, avoiding harmful substances, a clean environment, and the difference between a symptom and a sign of illness.
concepts.idea: A healthy lifestyle plus a clean environment keeps us well; a symptom is what we feel and a sign is what can be seen or measured.
concepts.rule: To stay healthy we should eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruits, vegetables and whole grains, avoid processed, fatty or sugary food and drinks, stay physically active, limit screen time, get enough sleep, practise yoga or breathing exercises such as pranayama, and say no to harmful substances like tobacco, alcohol and addictive drugs. Keeping our surroundings clean also matters: air pollution from vehicles and factories can cause coughing or asthma, and the Air Quality Index (AQI) tells us how clean the air is. A cleaner environment helps us stay healthy. Health is also about feelings and relationships, so spending time with friends and family helps keep our minds healthy. When we feel unwell, we may notice symptoms, which are what we feel, such as pain or tiredness, and signs, which are what can be seen or measured, such as fever, rash or swelling.
concepts.example: Air pollution from vehicles and factories in a city can cause coughing or asthma, showing how a dirty environment affects health.

concepts.name: Diseases: causes, pathogens and communicable disease types
concepts.description: What causes diseases, the difference between communicable and non-communicable diseases, common pathogens, how communicable diseases spread (air, contact, food/water, vectors), and everyday precautions against them.
concepts.idea: Diseases caused by pathogens that spread from person to person are called communicable; disease-causing organisms are called pathogens, and insects that spread them are called vectors.
concepts.rule: A disease is a condition that affects the normal working of the body or mind. Some diseases are caused by pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, worms or protozoa; these are communicable diseases and can spread from one person to another. Other diseases, such as cancer, diabetes or asthma, are non-communicable: they are not caused by pathogens, do not spread between people, and are usually linked to lifestyle, diet or environment. Communicable diseases spread through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, through direct contact such as shaking hands, indirectly by sharing personal items, through contaminated food or water, and by vectors such as mosquitoes and houseflies that carry pathogens between people. Examples include common cold and influenza (virus, respiratory tract), chickenpox and measles (virus), tuberculosis (bacteria, lungs), Hepatitis A (virus, liver), cholera and typhoid (bacteria, intestine), ascariasis or roundworm infection (worms, intestine), and malaria and dengue (spread by mosquitoes). Simple precautions such as washing hands, covering the mouth and nose, avoiding sharing personal items, keeping food and water clean, staying home when unwell, and controlling mosquito breeding help prevent these diseases from spreading.
concepts.example: An infected person coughing near others can spread the common cold virus through the air to healthy people nearby.

concepts.name: Non-communicable diseases: deficiency and chronic diseases
concepts.description: Non-communicable diseases caused by lack of nutrients (deficiency diseases) or by long-term lifestyle and environmental factors (chronic diseases), including diabetes and its causes.
concepts.idea: Deficiency diseases are caused by a lack of specific nutrients, while chronic diseases persist for a long time and are linked to lifestyle, diet or environment rather than pathogens.
concepts.rule: Some non-communicable diseases, such as scurvy, anaemia and goitre, are caused by a lack of specific nutrients in the diet and are called deficiency diseases. Diseases such as cancer, diabetes and asthma often persist for more than three months and are called chronic diseases. Diabetes is a common disease becoming more prevalent in adults and children; it often develops due to a combination of hormonal imbalances, unhealthy eating habits, lack of physical activity, and being overweight or obese. In recent years, non-communicable diseases like diabetes, heart disease and cancer have become more common in India because of changes in how people live, such as eating more processed food, getting less exercise, and living longer lives. Today, most deaths in India are caused by non-communicable diseases.
concepts.example: A child who does not get enough vitamin C in the diet can develop scurvy, a deficiency disease.

concepts.name: Prevention: immunity and vaccines
concepts.description: How the body's immune system fights disease, what immunity and vaccines are, how vaccines are made, and Edward Jenner's discovery of the smallpox vaccine.
concepts.idea: Immunity is the body's natural ability to fight disease, and vaccines train the immune system to recognise and fight pathogens, giving acquired immunity.
concepts.rule: The natural ability of our body to fight diseases is called immunity, provided by the immune system. Vaccines help the body fight certain diseases by training the immune system to recognise and attack harmful germs, giving acquired immunity, which is protection developed after exposure to a pathogen or a vaccine. Vaccines can be made from weakened or dead pathogens, from inactive or harmless parts of the pathogen, or by instructing body cells to make a harmless part of the germ for the immune system to learn to fight; a tetanus shot, for example, contains an inactivated bacterial toxin. Vaccines are preventive, not curative: they help stop serious diseases before they happen but do not cure someone who is already sick. In the late 1700s, English doctor Edward Jenner observed that people who had caught the milder disease cowpox did not get smallpox. He tested this by injecting cowpox sap into a boy, who later showed no illness when exposed to smallpox, leading to the invention of the first vaccine and helping eradicate smallpox worldwide by 1979. India is one of the world's largest vaccine producers and supplies vaccines to many countries.
concepts.example: A tetanus shot given after an injury contains an inactivated bacterial toxin that trains the immune system without causing the disease.

questions.q: Describe, in order, how Edward Jenner's observation, hypothesis, experiment and result led to the world's first vaccine.
questions.a: Jenner observed that milkmaids with cowpox did not catch smallpox; he hypothesised that content in the cowpox sores protected people from smallpox; he tested this by injecting cowpox sap into a boy; the boy showed no illness when later exposed to smallpox, leading to the invention of the first vaccine.

questions.q: Compare how acquired immunity develops after catching a disease naturally versus after receiving a vaccine for the same disease.
questions.a: Catching a disease naturally exposes the immune system to the actual pathogen, which can also cause illness or complications while the body builds immunity; a vaccine exposes the immune system to a weakened, dead or harmless part of the pathogen, training it to recognise and fight the disease without causing the illness itself.

questions.q: Some people fear or doubt vaccines. Do you think this fear is justified, based on what you have read? Justify your answer.

concepts.name: Treatment: antibiotics and antibiotic resistance
concepts.description: How antibiotics treat bacterial infections, why they do not work against viruses, and how overuse and incomplete doses lead to antibiotic resistance.
concepts.idea: Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work against viruses or protozoa, and using them incorrectly or unnecessarily leads to antibiotic resistance.
concepts.rule: If the immune system fails to protect us, a doctor may give antibiotics, medicines that kill bacteria causing an infection. Antibiotics work only against bacterial infections because they target parts of bacterial cells that are different from human or other animal cells; they do not work against viruses or diseases caused by protozoa. Penicillin, the first antibiotic, was discovered in 1928 by Alexander Fleming, who noticed that a mould on a discarded petri dish stopped bacteria from growing. Although antibiotics have saved millions of lives, their indiscriminate use has led to antibiotic resistance, a phenomenon where bacteria that were earlier killed by a given antibiotic survive and multiply despite treatment with it. This happens when antibiotics are taken when not required, or when a course is left incomplete, allowing surviving bacteria to develop and spread resistance among people, animals and the environment. To reduce antibiotic resistance, antibiotics should be used only when prescribed by a doctor, in the correct dose, and for the right duration. Traditional medicine systems like Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani have long been used in India to manage common health problems using natural substances and a focus on lifestyle, but they may not be effective for all diseases and at all stages.
concepts.example: Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould growing on a petri dish stopped bacteria from growing nearby, leading to the discovery of penicillin.

questions.q: Explain how overuse of antibiotics in both humans and animals can lead to antibiotic-resistant bacteria spreading through a community, using the chapter's description.
questions.a: When antibiotics are used unnecessarily or incompletely in humans or animals, a few bacteria develop resistance and survive; these resistant bacteria can spread through direct contact, hospital surfaces, food from treated animals, or contaminated soil and water, eventually spreading resistant infections through the community.

questions.q: Compare how Alexander Fleming's discovery of penicillin helped treat disease with how the overuse of antibiotics has since created a new problem.
questions.a: Fleming's discovery of penicillin gave doctors an effective way to kill bacteria and treat infections that were once deadly, saving millions of lives. However, using antibiotics too often or incorrectly since then has led some bacteria to develop resistance, making these same antibiotics less effective and some infections harder to treat again.

questions.q: A friend says, 'Antibiotics can cure any infection, so we do not need to worry about diseases.' Do you agree? Justify your answer.

questions.q: Design three rules for a 'smart antibiotic use' poster to help reduce antibiotic resistance in your community.
questions.a: For example: only take antibiotics when prescribed by a doctor, always complete the full course even if you feel better, and never share leftover antibiotics with others.
